90.bp: When companies deploy AI systems like ChatGPT to handle sensitive web tasks—summarizing private information, generating FAQ pages, or filtering user comments—those outputs need to be both useful and trustworthy. The real-world goal is to ship systems that protect people's privacy while getting accurate work done, so that users can rely on what the AI says without fear of data leaks or harmful mistakes.
90.wh: The obvious thing to do is write a prompt and hope it works, but that fails in practice: the AI might accidentally include personal details, generate misleading content, or fail in ways that break a website's policy. There's no built-in scorecard to say 'this prompt is ready to ship' or 'this one isn't', and each mistake can damage real users and the company's trust.
90.ap: This tutorial teaches a repeatable workflow: start with simple prompts, layer on specific rules (like 'never include phone numbers'), test them against a handful of real examples and deliberate edge cases that an adversary might exploit, then bundle those prompts with a checklist covering privacy, consent, and what to log. Participants learn techniques like asking the AI to reason through its work before answering, taking on a specific role, and chaining multiple questions together; they also learn when to plug the AI into external tools or databases for grounded facts.
90.ww: Small guardrails early catch the most obvious failures; testing with adversarial examples reveals blind spots the designer wouldn't think of alone. By forcing the prompt into a defensive role—asking it to explain its reasoning or asking it to refuse unsafe tasks—you shift the AI toward caution rather than just speed. And creating a deployment checklist makes it concrete: if you can't fill in the metrics, you're not ready yet.
90.po: Participants walk away able to ship production prompts that are defensible (you can explain why you made each choice), privacy-safe (you've thought through what not to leak), and testable (you have a rubric and known failure cases). The tutorial gives concrete artifacts: prompt cards, a scoring rubric, and a one-page deployment readiness form.

91.bp: From the earliest days of the Web, the thing we were trying to make work has changed dramatically. At first, success meant 'can I find the document I need quickly?'—a retrieval problem, like a library catalog. Over decades, as billions of people came online and the Web exploded with content, success shifted to 'did I feel satisfied? was the experience useful? did I keep coming back?'—a much softer, longer-term goal about the whole human experience.
91.wh: The tension is that searching for the 'most relevant document' and creating an experience that keeps someone engaged are almost opposite problems. The first is measurable in seconds—did you find it yes or no?—and is solved by ranking documents better. The second is soft and sprawls over weeks or months: did this platform respect my time? did it show me things that genuinely mattered? You can't measure that in a lab anymore.
91.ap: The talk traces how the Web industry adapted: early searchers optimized for relevance ranking; then platforms noticed that relevance alone wasn't enough—context matters, knowing the person's true intent matters, trust matters. So they added personalization, feeds that adapt to what you engage with, social signals. When AI came along, it accelerated the trend by making it possible to reason about intent more deeply and to build experiences that adapt in real time.
91.ww: As content abundance exploded, the old approach broke: showing the most literally relevant document doesn't actually solve anyone's real problem if there are a million equally relevant documents. The platform had to shift to 'what does this person actually want and care about?' and 'what will keep them coming back?', which requires tracking longer-term signals (engagement, retention, whether they find it useful weeks later) rather than one-click success metrics.
91.po: The talk reframes how we should think about Web systems: success isn't just relevance anymore, it's sustained value and user intent-awareness. This explains why recommender systems and feeds dominate the modern Web, and why AI that can reason about intent and adapt to individual users has become central to Web design, not a nice-to-have.

92.bp: When you shop on a marketplace like Alibaba and search using an image (rather than typing words), the system needs to understand not just what the product looks like visually but what it actually is and what it does. Getting this right matters because a wrong result frustrates the shopper, and in business-to-business contexts, a recommendation for the wrong product type can cause real operational damage or safety problems.
92.wh: The naive approach is 'find products that look visually similar to the image', but that's a trap: a silver ring and a silver coin look nearly identical but are completely different products. The system confidently returns the wrong thing. The harder problem is that visual similarity is easy to measure (pixels match), but semantic similarity (these are both rings, or these are both jewelry, or more specifically these are both wedding rings) requires understanding categories and subtle differences that go way beyond appearance.
92.ap: ARCHER breaks the problem into three stages, building up understanding step by step. First, it learns basic visual-text relationships (if you search with an image of a ring, anchor to words like 'ring' and 'jewelry'). Second, it learns to recognize the same product from different angles and lighting, so the system doesn't get confused by a product shot at different angles. Third, it fine-tunes to distinguish between similar products within a category—telling a gold ring from a silver ring, or a wedding ring from a fashion ring.
92.ww: By separating the problem into coarse-to-fine stages, the system avoids trying to learn everything at once (which often fails). Learning broad category understanding first gives the system a foundation; then learning viewpoint robustness prevents variation from confusing it; then the fine-grained stage can focus on subtle differences without noise. It's like learning to recognize 'animals' first, then 'cats', then 'tabby cats with white spots'—each stage is easier when the earlier work is done.
92.po: ARCHER returns products that are semantically correct—the same kind of thing, in the same category—rather than just visually close. For a business customer looking for industrial components, this prevents costly mistakes. For a consumer, search becomes actually usable rather than frustrating, because the top result is usually the type of thing they meant, not just something that happens to match the pixels.

93.bp: Online platforms like social media, review sites, and marketplaces are targets for organized fraud: groups of fake accounts work together to inflate review scores, game recommendation systems, or spread misinformation at scale. Detecting these collusive spam rings is crucial to keep platforms trustworthy and users safe, because an individual fake review is obvious, but a coordinated campaign of twenty reviews is much harder to spot.
93.wh: The standard approach treats fraud detection as a binary classification task—is this review spam or not?—but that misses the signal. A single fake review inside a sea of real ones is hard to identify. The real issue is that fraudsters work in groups, and the group's behavior—patterns in timing, language, the accounts that interact with each other—is the smoking gun. Existing methods look at individual accounts in isolation, missing the forest for the trees.
93.ap: SetDet redefines the problem: instead of asking 'is this one review fake?', it asks 'which groups of reviews look coordinated and fraudulent?'. It learns representations of entire sets of reviews together, capturing the group dynamics—do these accounts always interact together? do their reviews use similar language? are the timings suspicious?—and then makes a group-level decision: 'this cluster is collusion, that one is legitimate.' The framework jointly learns what fraud looks like (the representation) and makes the detection decision at the same time, so they inform each other.
93.ww: Fraud is fundamentally a group phenomenon: it's the coordination and collective dynamics that make it fraud. Looking at individual reviews misses the temporal patterns (all posting at 3am), the linguistic patterns (same phrasing across accounts), and the interaction patterns (same set of users always review the same products). By making the group the unit of analysis and learning at that level, the system can catch behaviors that are invisible at the individual level.
93.po: SetDet can identify organized fraud rings that current methods miss, because it looks for the signature of coordination rather than individual oddities. This means real spam campaigns can be caught and removed, preserving the integrity of review systems and recommendation algorithms, and protecting both the platform and honest users from manipulation.

94.bp: Knowledge graphs—structures that store facts as relationships between entities, like 'Alice works at Google'—are increasingly built by combining information from multiple organizations (hospitals, universities, companies) while keeping their data private. But if a malicious participant injects false information into the shared knowledge graph, the entire system's usefulness collapses. Stopping these attacks is crucial to keep federated knowledge systems trustworthy.
94.wh: The challenge is that federated systems trade centralized control for privacy: no single authority sees all the data, so no one person can easily spot when an attacker has poisoned the system. A traditional centralized knowledge graph could be audited; here, the attack might be hidden in one participant's contribution and spread through the network before anyone notices. Existing defenses for centralized systems don't work when you can't see all the data.
94.ap: This paper designs three attack strategies that a malicious participant might use: some corrupt the raw data before it goes into the system, others corrupt the learned representations (the underlying math structures) the system builds. They show that corrupting the representations is the most effective attack. Then they propose a defense: monitor the 'density' of the learned representations (how tightly packed the math structures are), since poisoned data tends to create anomalous density patterns that signal an attack. A monitoring system flags suspicious participants and removes their contributions.
94.ww: Poisoned data tends to distort the learned structures in detectable ways: the math model learns to fit the false information, and that distortion shows up as unusual density or clustering patterns. By monitoring for these anomalies in the mathematical space (rather than trying to audit the raw data, which you can't see), the system can catch attacks without breaking privacy. The poisoned representations stand out like a sore thumb in the learned model.
94.po: The defense can restore a federated knowledge graph to pre-attack performance even after a severe poisoning campaign that dropped accuracy by 93%. This means organizations can confidently share data through a federated knowledge system—they know that if someone poisons it, the system can detect and fix the damage automatically.

95.bp: Recommendation systems learn patterns from data to suggest products or content you might like. But the real world is messy: patterns that worked during training break when users see a new product type or when the market shifts. A system trained on summer fashion recommendations fails when winter comes. Building recommenders that stay accurate when the world changes is a hard real-world problem that directly affects whether people trust the recommendations.
95.wh: The issue is that recommender systems exploit correlations in the training data—'people who bought ski pants also bought thermal socks'—but those correlations can be accidents of the training set, not real causal truths about what people want. When the data distribution shifts (winter ends, new product types arrive), those spurious correlations fall apart and the recommendations become garbage. The system was optimizing for correlation, not for understanding the causal reasons behind choices.
95.ap: C-HyPOD uses a mathematical trick: it learns to place user interests in hyperbolic space, a kind of geometry that naturally captures hierarchies (imagine a tree structure embedded in space, where each level is a different layer of specificity). Instead of learning scattered features, it learns a small set of universal interest 'archetypes' (prototypes) arranged hierarchically, and it ensures those archetypes are orthogonal—they don't overlap, so each one captures something distinct. When distribution shifts happen, these fundamental archetypes are more likely to transfer correctly because they're aligned with real causal structures, not accidental correlations.
95.ww: Hyperbolic geometry is good at capturing hierarchies—from broad interests ('outdoor activities') down to specific ones ('cross-country skiing in March')—which mirrors how real user preferences actually structure themselves. By learning prototypes that are orthogonal (truly distinct from each other) rather than overlapping, the system learns reusable causal building blocks. When the data distribution shifts, these fundamental units are more robust because they represent true structure, not just data accidents.
95.po: C-HyPOD recommendations stay accurate when product catalogs change, when seasons shift, or when new user cohorts arrive—situations where naive recommenders fail badly. This means recommendation systems can be deployed to real marketplaces and stay helpful over time, rather than degrading as the world changes.

96.bp: When you ask a large language model (LLM) like GPT-4 a question about facts stored in a knowledge graph—'Who was the first president of the United States and where was he from?'—the model often makes up an answer rather than admitting it doesn't know. Combining knowledge graphs (which have reliable facts) with LLMs (which can reason) should solve this, but most systems don't work well for smaller models, which are cheaper and easier to deploy.
96.wh: Existing knowledge graph question-answering systems are built for the biggest models; they feed raw knowledge graph paths (chains of relationships) directly into the model and hope it can figure out which ones matter. Smaller models struggle with this: they don't have the raw reasoning power to sort through noise, and they're not trained to handle the knowledge graph's structure. It's like handing someone a jumbled library and expecting them to find the answer—it works better for genius researchers than for ordinary people.
96.ap: RPO-RAG does three things: First, it samples knowledge graph paths more carefully, choosing ones that are actually relevant to the question (not just random paths). Second, it trains the small model specifically on reasoning about relationships in the knowledge graph—showing it what 'president of' means, how to navigate 'lived in', so it learns to manipulate these concepts. Third, it organizes the retrieved paths into a clear, interpretable format before asking the model to answer, so the model isn't overwhelmed by noise.
96.ww: Smaller models succeed when the problem is broken down: if you give it clear, relevant examples of 'here's a path through the knowledge graph that answers a similar question', it can learn to imitate that pattern. By teaching it specifically about relationships (which is what knowledge graphs are made of) and filtering the retrieved paths before they reach the model, you've done half the work. The model's limited reasoning capacity goes toward the right thing, not toward filtering noise.
96.po: Small LLMs (under 7 billion parameters) can now answer factual questions about knowledge graphs as accurately as much larger models, because they're trained and presented with the right structure. This is a big deal for deployment: smaller models are cheaper, faster, and can run on consumer hardware, so this makes factual question-answering practical in real applications where GPT-4 is too expensive.

97.bp: Misinformation spreads across the web, but every new crisis—COVID, a war, an election—changes what false claims look like. A system trained to catch COVID misinformation might miss war-related falsehoods because the patterns and language are completely different. Building systems that detect fake news in unseen crises is crucial because once a major event happens, there's no time to retrain.
97.wh: The problem is that fake news in one context uses different language, appeals to different emotions, and exploits different knowledge gaps than in another. A system trained on one domain learns very specific features of that domain's misinformation. When a new crisis hits, those features don't transfer. Additionally, labeled data is scarce—you can't quickly gather thousands of labeled examples of COVID misinformation about a new topic. And LLMs understand abstract meaning but that understanding doesn't always transfer across domains either.
97.ap: DAUD uses LLMs to extract high-level meaning from both news articles (the semantic content, the framing, the implicit claims) and user comments (who's engaging with this, what they're saying). It then models how individual users engage with news across different domains—if someone always shares misinformation about vaccines, they're more likely to share misinformation about a new health crisis. It captures the relationship between the original article features and the LLM-extracted features, so the LLM's understanding can enhance the system without completely replacing the data-driven signals.
97.ww: LLMs understand abstract meaning that's more likely to transfer across domains—the narrative structure of false claims, emotional manipulation patterns—than surface-level features do. User behavior is even more transferable: someone's tendency to share misinformation is often domain-agnostic. By combining LLM-extracted semantics with user behavioral signals and grounding everything in the original data-driven features, the system captures both domain-specific and domain-agnostic aspects of misinformation, allowing knowledge to transfer to unseen crises.
97.po: DAUD can detect misinformation in new, unseen contexts (new geopolitical crises, new pandemics) better than systems trained on old domains, because it captures the abstract patterns of false claims and the user behaviors that spread them. This means during a real crisis, the system can start catching misinformation immediately rather than waiting weeks for labeled training data.

98.bp: The internet runs on foundational security measures—encryption, authentication, domain validation—that are mature, well-understood, and freely available. Yet many services don't use them. Understanding how widely these basic protections are deployed across the real internet is essential for knowing how resilient the internet actually is and where to focus efforts to improve security.
98.wh: The obvious thing—ask services to report—doesn't work because it's voluntary and people lie or don't know. The hard part is measuring this at scale without breaking into systems or being intrusive. You need a way to check security measures by looking from outside, without annoying anyone or getting in legal trouble, and you need to do it for hundreds of thousands of domains.
98.ap: The paper proposes a set of security indicators that can be checked non-intrusively: Does this domain have DNSSEC (encrypted DNS)? Does it support HTTPS (encrypted web traffic)? Does it have a security policy file? These are all things you can check by looking at publicly available information or making normal network requests. They built a tool called Katti and checked every known .de domain (German internet) to see who's using these measures.
98.ww: By focusing on foundational, standardized measures that are both mature and non-intrusively measurable, they can get a broad, accurate picture of internet security without requiring cooperation or breaking systems. These indicators are lagging indicators—many of them have existed for 10+ years—so if services still aren't using them, that's informative. It's like checking 'do you have locks on your doors'—not fancy, but critical.
98.po: The study reveals that a significant chunk of the German internet still lacks even basic security measures. This makes clear where the gap between knowledge and practice lies and where sustained attention is needed to improve internet resilience, not just innovation on new security tricks but deployment of things we've known for years.

99.bp: False information spreads online when images and text are manipulated together. A real photo of a protest might be paired with a false caption claiming something happened that didn't, or an AI-generated image might be paired with authentic reporting to make it seem real. Detecting these multi-layered falsehoods is crucial because our brains trust images more than words, and when image plus text combine to lie, the effect is especially powerful.
99.wh: The problem is that existing methods treat multimodal misinformation as a single classification task ('true or false'), but that misses the real structure. An image can be real and text false, or both false, or both real but paired to tell a lie—these are different problems requiring different solutions. No single classifier handles all cases well. Additionally, covering all possible combinations is complicated; researchers have mostly focused on a few common cases and missed the full space of possibilities.
99.ap: OctantFake proposes a simpler framework: Check the image independently (real or fake?), check the text independently (real or fake?), check whether they're consistent with each other (does the text match what the image shows?). This creates eight possible combinations: real-image + real-text + consistent means true; fake-image + real-text + inconsistent means false; and so on. They built a large dataset covering all eight cases and trained separate specialized modules for each check, then fused the results into a final classification.
99.ww: By separating the problem into three independent checks, you sidestep the impossibility of one-size-fits-all detection. An image analysis expert's tool can focus on image forensics; a text analysis expert's tool can focus on text truth; a consistency checker can focus on alignment. Each module can be simpler and more accurate because it's solving a narrower problem. Fusing three moderately accurate answers is more robust than chasing one complex answer.
99.po: OctantFake can detect multimodal misinformation that combines real and fake elements in ways previous systems missed, because it explicitly handles all eight combinations rather than trying to brute-force a single classifier. This means fact-checkers and platforms can catch sophisticated hybrid lies that mix real images with false claims or vice versa.

100.bp: When you read reviews or news, you often care about a specific angle: 'Is the product's battery life good?' or 'Does this writer think the policy is fair?' Extracting opinion about a specific aspect from text is called aspect-based sentiment analysis, and it matters for product review sites, policy monitoring, and customer feedback. But models can be fooled by surface patterns and don't actually understand what they're analyzing.
100.wh: The trap is that models learn shortcuts: they notice that words like 'disappointing' usually appear near negative reviews and 'excellent' near positive ones, so they predict based on word patterns alone. But this fails when the pattern is misleading: 'not bad' means positive, but contains the word 'bad'. More fundamentally, models can learn spurious correlations—'this product appears in luxury reviews so all reviews in this category must be positive'—that work on training data but fail on new data.
100.ap: CECR uses counterfactual reasoning: take a real review, then create fake variations of it where you change the target aspect you're analyzing but keep everything else the same. For example, if the original says 'This phone's battery is great but the screen sucks', create a counterfactual where you swap in 'This phone's battery is terrible but the screen sucks', and note that the opinion should flip. Train the model on both versions so it learns that the aspect itself causes the opinion, not surrounding words. At inference time, use a causal attention mechanism that identifies which parts of the text actually influence the prediction.
100.ww: Counterfactuals force the model to learn causal relationships: if I change the battery description, the sentiment must change. That rules out spurious shortcuts because the shortcut (the word 'bad' appears) is the same in both versions, but the label changes. Causal attention mechanisms help the model zero in on the words and phrases that are actually causally driving the prediction, not just correlating with it.
100.po: CECR is more robust than standard models: it handles tricky phrasings like 'not bad' correctly, and it generalizes better to new data because it learned causal relationships rather than shortcuts. For a review site trying to understand customer opinions accurately, this means the system gives reliable feedback even on unusual phrasing and isn't easily fooled by changes in how reviewers write.

101.bp: Complex networks like the internet or social media can fail in ways we need to understand: a virus spreading through a network, misinformation cascading through links, infrastructure collapse when key hubs go down. The network dismantling problem asks: if we wanted to stop a cascade or disable the most damaging part of the network, which nodes (people, servers, websites) would we need to remove with minimum cost? This matters for both defense (stopping epidemics) and infrastructure planning (where are the critical chokepoints).
101.wh: Naively, you'd remove the most-connected nodes (hubs) first, but that's inefficient. The network might have a giant connected component (a huge interlinked mass) plus scattered small clusters. You don't need to remove nodes until the giant component fragments. Finding the minimal removal strategy is mathematically hard—it's a classic NP-hard problem, meaning there's no known fast algorithm that always finds the true optimum.
101.ap: IG+ starts with a clever flip in perspective: instead of asking 'which nodes should I remove?', it asks 'if I'm keeping nodes, which should I keep to maintain connectivity?' By finding the nodes worth keeping (the ones that hold the network together), it identifies implicitly which ones to remove. This reverse perspective often makes optimization problems easier. The algorithm uses heuristics (fast approximations) and for dynamic networks, uses tree-based data structures to update the dismantling strategy when nodes are added or removed.
101.ww: The reverse perspective works because the structure of the problem is actually clearer when framed as 'what's the smallest set that stays connected?' rather than 'what's the biggest set I can destroy?' For dynamic networks, maintaining a tree-based index lets you avoid recomputing from scratch every time the network changes—you just update the index, which is much faster.
101.po: IG+ can dismantle 10-million-node networks in minutes and handle changes as they happen. This makes it practical for real systems: understanding which infrastructure chokepoints matter most, planning for network resilience, or simulating how misinformation cascades would be stopped by targeted interventions.

102.bp: The internet is evolving toward a new era where artificial intelligence and blockchain combine, where privacy and verifiability are central, and where quantum computers pose a threat to existing security. Building systems that are decentralized (no single authority can control you), private (no one can see your data), and quantum-safe (they'll still work when quantum computers exist) is the goal. But it requires rethinking identity, trust, and how we prove things online.
102.wh: The challenge is that these three goals—decentralization, privacy, quantum-resistance—have often pulled in different directions. A decentralized system is harder to audit. A quantum-safe system requires new math that's unfamiliar. Privacy and verifiability seem to conflict: how do you prove something happened if you don't reveal who you are? There's no clear roadmap for how to build systems that achieve all three, and there are no standard benchmarks or failure-mode catalogs to learn from.
102.ap: ZABAPAD is a workshop bringing together practitioners working on these problems. It focuses on real deployments and empirical measurements rather than theory alone. It explores zero-knowledge proofs (a way to prove you know something without revealing it) combined with blockchain, applies these ideas to IoT devices that need to authenticate themselves, and examines what happens when you need to migrate existing digital identities and wallets to quantum-safe systems. It aims to produce a practitioner playbook, an interoperability checklist, benchmarks, and a catalog of failure modes across domains like finance, healthcare, and supply chain.
102.ww: Progress happens when practitioners share what failed, not just what worked. By collecting empirical benchmarks and failure modes across real deployments in finance, healthcare, and supply chain, the workshop creates a knowledge base that future builders can learn from. Zero-knowledge proofs are powerful tools for privacy-preserving verification, and blockchain provides the decentralization; combining them with quantum-safe math and mapping out the integration points is how you actually build next-generation systems.
102.po: The workshop outcomes are concrete: teams leave with a playbook for how to adopt zero-knowledge proof and blockchain technologies in their domain, a checklist for making sure systems from different builders can interoperate, benchmarks for comparing approaches, and most importantly, a collection of 'here's where previous projects stumbled' lessons that help new projects avoid the same pitfalls.

103.bp: The protocols that run the internet—how data is transmitted, how computers talk to each other, how security works—are written down in documents called RFCs (Requests for Comments). These are the law of the internet. But reading an RFC is often cryptic: it tells you the rules, but not why those rules exist or what tradeoff led to them. Understanding the reasoning would make protocols easier to implement correctly and to understand why they work.
103.wh: The knowledge of why protocols were designed a certain way lives in email archives and meeting notes from protocol working groups, scattered across years of discussion. Most RFC readers never see this context. They read the rule, don't understand the tradeoff, misinterpret the spec, and implement it wrong. It's like having a legal document but no case law or legislative history—you can follow the letter but miss the spirit.
103.ap: This paper builds a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system tailored for RFC design rationales. It digs through IETF email archives and working group discussions to find relevant context, then uses a language model to synthesize that context into a clear explanation of why a protocol decision was made and what constraints it addresses. The key innovation is in the retriever: it's tuned to find emails that actually contain rationale (not just routine discussion), and at large search scales, it's much better at returning the crucial context while keeping it brief to save tokens.
103.ww: RFC design rationales are buried in email, and not all emails are equally useful—most are routine discussion, only a few contain the actual 'we chose X because Y' reasoning. By training a specialized retriever to distinguish rationale-rich emails, the system can find the signal in the noise. Keeping contexts short makes the language model's synthesis task easier and cheaper, especially when searching across large email archives.
103.po: RFC readers can now look up not just the rule but the reasoning behind it, making standards more transparent and implementers more likely to get the design right. This is especially valuable for protocol authors and implementers debugging subtle spec ambiguities—they can understand the original intent, not just the words.

104.bp: In decentralized finance (DeFi), a clever trader can spot opportunities to profit: if a token is cheaper on one exchange than another, you can buy low and sell high, pocketing the difference. These arbitrage opportunities happen fast and at scale. Building systems that can automatically spot and execute profitable arbitrage trades is the goal, but it has to be done under real-world constraints: you have limited money, pools have limited liquidity, you have to pay for the transaction, and the opportunity disappears in milliseconds.
104.wh: Finding the best arbitrage path and trade amount is a nasty optimization problem: there are many possible sequences of trades (pools to route through), each with different profitability, and all have constraints (limited funds, pool liquidity, gas fees). The obvious approach—try every possibility—finds the best answer but takes too long to run; by the time you finish calculating, the opportunity is gone. You need something fast and good-enough that runs in milliseconds on a blockchain.
104.ap: The paper formulates atomic triangular arbitrage as a constrained optimization problem (select an ordered path of three pools and a trade amount to maximize profit) and solves it using Deep Reinforcement Learning with a specific algorithm called PPO. The model learns from experience: it observes the state (current pool prices, your balance, constraints), takes an action (pick a path and amount), gets a reward (profit or loss), and learns to repeat the profitable actions. The trained model runs in milliseconds because it's just neural network inference, not search.
104.ww: Neural networks can learn to approximate solutions to hard optimization problems much faster than solving them exactly. PPO is stable and sample-efficient, meaning it learns from relatively few examples. The network learns to navigate the constraint space (respecting your balance, avoiding pools with too little liquidity) while maximizing profit, all in a way that generalizes to new prices it hasn't seen before.
104.po: PPO achieves millisecond-level inference speed, making it practical for on-chain execution, while still generating consistent profit. This reveals a fundamental speed-profit tradeoff: exhaustive search finds the absolute best arbitrage but is too slow; PPO finds good arbitrage fast enough to actually execute, which in the real world is what matters. A reasonably profitable opportunity you can execute beats a theoretically optimal opportunity you can't.
